transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I’m having a really hard time finishing things all the way through at work, even things I know are important. I work in meat processing, and there are these sanitation steps, batch logs, and end-of-line paperwork that have to be done correctly, and I’ll start them, I’ll really think I’m doing them, but somehow I leave off the last part or miss the final steps.

It’s not that I don’t care, because I do—honestly, I get stressed about it because I know my job depends on doing those things right. But I’ll get partway through and then it’s like I move on too soon or lose the thread, and later I realize I didn’t actually finish the whole thing. It’s been happening enough that I felt like I needed to come in and talk to someone, because I don’t know why I keep doing that when I know better.
Do you find yourself having trouble finishing things or losing track of tasks outside of work as well?

Yeah, I mean… the biggest place I really notice it, and the reason I came in, is at work. That’s where it feels like it’s causing actual consequences. I’ll start the sanitation steps or I’ll be working through the batch logs or the end-of-line paperwork, and I honestly think I’m doing it properly, like I know these things matter and I know my job depends on finishing them correctly. But then somehow I leave out the last parts, or I don’t complete the final step, and I only realize later that it wasn’t actually finished.

It’s frustrating because it’s not like I’m choosing not to do it or thinking it’s unimportant. I’ll be partway through, and then something shifts and I’ve moved on, and the task is just… not all the way done. That’s the main thing I can point to clearly.
Are you experiencing any problems in your personal relationships due to these difficulties with finishing tasks?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I haven’t noticed it in the same clear way I notice it at work. Like, with work there are specific steps and paperwork, so it’s obvious when I didn’t finish something. In my personal life, it’s harder for me to tell if it’s causing problems with people or if I’m just kind of overthinking things.

I don’t have a specific relationship issue that comes to mind where someone has said, “You never finish things,” or anything like that. I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed major problems there, at least not enough that I can point to it clearly.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind that you can't seem to get rid of?

Um… not really, I don’t think so. I mean, I get stressed about things, especially if I know I messed something up or I’m worried I forgot a step, and I might think about it a lot afterward. But I don’t know if I’d call it thoughts repeating that I can’t get rid of.

Like, I don’t have a specific thought or phrase that keeps looping in my head over and over for no reason, at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more just normal worrying when something has gone wrong, I think. If you mean like intrusive thoughts or something that feels stuck no matter what I do, I don’t really think that’s happening to me.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety, like you can't sit still?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s a big thing for me. I mean, I can fidget a little like anyone, like shifting in a chair or messing with my hands if I’m sitting for a while, but I don’t really feel like I’m constantly driven to move or like I physically can’t sit still.

At work I’m on my feet a lot anyway, so it’s kind of hard to compare, because I’m moving around as part of the job. But if I’m sitting somewhere, like here or at home, I don’t usually feel like I have to jump up or pace around. So… no, I haven’t really noticed restlessness or fidgetiness as one of the main problems.
Do you have any habits or rituals that you feel compelled to do over and over?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I have routines for certain things, especially because at work there are things you’re supposed to do a certain way, but I don’t think I have anything where I feel like I have to repeat it over and over or something bad will happen.

At home, maybe I’ll double-check something once in a while, like whether I have my phone or keys, but it doesn’t feel like a ritual. It’s more just me trying not to forget something. I’m not stuck washing my hands repeatedly or checking locks again and again or counting things, if that’s what you mean.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed anything like compulsive habits or rituals.
Do you often feel anxious or nervous?

I mean… I get nervous sometimes, yeah, but I don’t know if I’d say I’m anxious all the time or anything like that. It kind of depends on what’s going on. Like if there’s something important happening, or if I think I might have done something wrong, I can definitely feel tense and keep thinking about it for a while.

But as a general thing, like walking around every day feeling nervous for no reason, I don’t think that’s really me. I’m not usually sitting there with my heart racing or feeling panicky. It’s more situation-based, I guess. If there’s a reason to be stressed, then I feel stressed, but I don’t think I’m constantly anxious.
Do you have trouble paying attention or following instructions in your daily life outside of work?

Yes. That’s actually a big part of why I’m here. Outside of the actual cutting or processing part, it’s the follow-through stuff that gets me, especially when there are steps that have to be finished in order.

Like with sanitation steps, or batch logs, or the end-of-line paperwork, I’ll start it, and I really do know it matters. It’s not like I don’t care or I don’t understand that it has to be done correctly. But somehow I’ll get through part of it and then leave off the last section, or miss the final piece, or think I completed it and then later realize I didn’t actually finish the whole thing.

And that’s really frustrating, because it’s the kind of thing where my job depends on doing it right. I know the instructions, and if someone asks me what I’m supposed to do, I can usually explain it. But in the moment, following it all the way through without dropping the last part is where I mess up. It feels like I’m constantly starting the process properly and then somehow not landing the plane, if that makes sense.
Do you have trouble organizing your tasks or activities?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because it depends what you mean by organizing. Like, if you mean do I have a planner system or a neat way I lay everything out, then… not really, honestly. I try to, but it doesn’t always stay that way.

I can usually understand what needs to happen, and I can sometimes make a list or tell myself, “Okay, first I’ll do this, then this, then this.” But actually keeping the tasks sorted in my head and moving through them in a clean order is harder. I’ll start one thing, then realize another thing is also important, then I kind of shift to that, and then I’m not always clear what I already finished versus what I only meant to finish.

Even at home, if I’m trying to get chores done or run errands, I can spend a lot of time just sort of circling the tasks instead of doing them in order. I’ll think, “I should do laundry,” but then I need to clear the floor, and then I notice dishes, and then I remember I was supposed to text someone back, and then somehow the original thing is still sitting there. It’s not that I’m trying to be disorganized, and I don’t feel like I’m lazy exactly—it feels more like I can’t keep the structure of the task together unless it’s really obvious or someone else is directing it.

So yes, I think I do have trouble organizing tasks and activities, but I guess I notice it most when there are multiple steps or when no one is telling me exactly what to do next.
Do you often feel guilty about things that happen?

I’m not sure I’d say “often” in a big, constant way. I do feel guilty sometimes, like if I realize I forgot something or I think I made things harder for someone else. Then I’ll kind of replay it in my head and feel bad about it.

But I don’t think I walk around feeling guilty all the time, or like everything is my fault. It’s more tied to specific things that happen. If I know I messed something up, or even if I’m worried I might have, then yeah, I can feel guilty about that. But not out of nowhere, if that makes sense.
Did you have trouble paying attention or completing assignments when you were in school?

Yes, I did. I mean, looking back, it was there pretty early, not just something that started as an adult.

My mom actually still has some of my old elementary school report cards, and I remember seeing one from around fourth grade where the teacher basically said I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork and turn in homework. That’s kind of the exact pattern I remember, too. I wasn’t usually confused by the lesson itself. Like, if the teacher explained something and I was actually tuned in, I could understand it. But then when it came time to follow all the directions, or finish the worksheet, or remember to put the homework in the right place and actually hand it in, that’s where things would fall apart.

I remember missing parts of instructions a lot unless the teacher was nearby or kind of checking on me. If she was close to me, I could stay on track better, but if she gave the whole class directions and then moved on, I’d realize halfway through that I had missed a chunk of what we were supposed to do. It was embarrassing, because I didn’t feel like I didn’t know the material. It was more like I lost pieces of the process somewhere between hearing it and actually completing it.
Did you often feel like you were constantly on the go or had a lot of excess energy when you were a child?

I’m not really sure that fits me, honestly. I don’t remember being the kind of kid who was constantly running around or seemed like I had endless energy. I mean, I was a child, so I’m sure I had normal kid energy at times, like playing or getting excited, but I don’t think people described me as always “on the go” or unable to slow down.

If anything, when I think back, that’s not the part that stands out. I wasn’t usually the kid bouncing off the walls or needing to move nonstop. I’d have to ask my mom to be totally sure, because childhood memories are kind of blurry, but from what I remember, no, I don’t think I had a lot of excess energy in that way.
Do you feel like your difficulties with finishing tasks and following through on instructions are causing significant problems in your life outside of work?

I mean… yes, definitely. The biggest place I notice it is work, honestly, and it’s gotten to the point where it feels serious, not just annoying or like “oh, I’m forgetful.”

I work in a setting where there are steps and instructions that actually matter, and when I don’t finish something all the way or I miss part of what I was told, it doesn’t just affect me. Other people end up having to step in and cover pieces of my duties, or double-check things I should have already done. And that’s embarrassing, because I’m not trying to be careless. I really want to be reliable.

There have been formal retraining meetings because of it, where they go back over procedures with me, and I’ll understand it in the meeting, but then in the actual flow of work I’ll lose track of some part of it or not follow through the way I’m supposed to. It makes me feel like people are watching me like I’m a problem.

And I’m honestly scared I could be moved off the line or even fired if it keeps happening. That’s probably the part that weighs on me the most. I don’t want to be seen as a safety concern, but that’s kind of how it feels sometimes, like instead of being the dependable worker I’m trying to be, I’m becoming someone everyone has to work around.
Have you noticed any problems in your relationships with friends or family that you think might be related to your difficulties with finishing tasks or following instructions?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I haven’t really connected it as clearly with friends or family the way I have with work.

Like, with family, I’m sure there are times where I forget something someone asked me to do, or I don’t follow through right away, but I don’t know if I’d say it’s caused major relationship problems. I guess my family might get annoyed with me sometimes, but I haven’t really thought of it as this big pattern in the same way.

With friends, I don’t know… I don’t think anyone has directly said, like, “you’re a bad friend because you don’t finish things” or anything like that. Maybe there are little things, like if I say I’ll look something up or handle a plan and then I forget, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. It’s harder for me to separate normal forgetfulness from something that’s actually affecting the relationship.

So I guess my answer is I haven’t noticed it in a major way, or at least no one has really pointed it out to me like that.
Did you often act on impulse when you were younger, doing things without thinking them through?

I’m not really sure. I don’t have a strong memory of being especially impulsive as a kid, at least not in the sense of constantly doing risky things or acting without any thought at all.

I mean, I’m sure I did normal kid things where I made a quick decision or didn’t think something through, because I think most kids do that sometimes. But if you’re asking whether it was a noticeable pattern, like people were always saying I was impulsive or I was always getting into trouble because I acted too fast, I don’t really remember that being the case.

It’s a little hard because childhood memories are fuzzy, and I don’t know what my parents or teachers would say if you asked them directly. But from what I can remember, I wouldn’t describe myself as someone who was constantly acting on impulse when I was younger.
Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or activities when you're not at work?

Yes… I do. I mean, I notice it most at work because that’s where the consequences are more obvious, but it’s not like my focus problems only switch on when I clock in.

Even when I start a shift telling myself, like, “Okay, today I’m going to stay really locked in, I’m going to pay attention to every step,” after a while everything starts to kind of blend together. The cutting, weighing, checking labels, looking at the tray, looking at the log sheet… it all starts to blur, and then I’ll suddenly realize I’ve just been staring at the same tray or the same paperwork without actually taking in what I’m supposed to do next.

It’s not that I’m choosing not to focus. I’ll be looking right at the thing, but my brain isn’t fully grabbing onto it. Then I have to almost restart in my head and figure out, “Wait, what step was I on? Did I already check that? What was I supposed to do after this?” It’s really frustrating because I can start out trying so hard, and then I still drift off mentally.
Do you often avoid tasks or activities because you feel overwhelmed by them?

Yes, definitely. I think “overwhelmed” is actually a pretty accurate word for it, because it’s not always that the task is technically impossible or even that long, but the amount of mental effort it feels like it’s going to take makes me avoid it.

The biggest example is the certification modules and long procedure readings I’m supposed to do. I put those off until the absolute last possible minute. I’ll know I need to do them, and I’ll even have time, but just the idea of sitting there and trying to absorb all those rules and steps and wording feels almost physically exhausting. Like I’m tired before I even start. I’ll open it and see pages of procedures or training information, and my brain kind of goes, “Nope, not right now,” even if I know avoiding it is going to make things worse later.

And then I end up doing this whole thing where I tell myself I’ll do it after I eat, or after I shower, or when I’m more awake, or on my next day off, and then suddenly it’s right before it’s due and I’m trying to cram through it. It’s frustrating because I’m not avoiding it because I don’t care. I do care. It just feels so heavy to start, especially when I know I have to sit still and actually take in detailed information.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time on details, to the point where it slows down your completion of tasks?

I’m not totally sure. I don’t think that’s the main thing that slows me down, if that makes sense.

Like, I can get stuck on a detail sometimes if I’m worried I missed something, but I wouldn’t say I’m usually being perfectionistic or spending forever making something exactly right. It’s more that I lose track of where I am, or I have to reread or recheck because I’m not confident I actually took it in the first time.

So… if you mean, do I get so focused on tiny details that I can’t finish because I’m over-polishing everything, I don’t really think so. But if you mean I end up taking longer because I have to keep going back over things or checking what I already did, then maybe sometimes. I just don’t know if that counts as “spending a lot of time on details,” exactly.
Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or have symptoms of ADHD as a child, such as difficulty paying attention or hyperactivity?

I was never officially diagnosed as a kid, no. At least not that I know of. But looking back, there were definitely signs, especially with paying attention.

My mom actually still has some of my old elementary school report cards, and I remember one from around fourth grade saying something like I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork and turn in homework. That kind of sums up a lot of it, honestly. I wasn’t a kid who didn’t understand what was being taught. I usually did understand the lesson once I was actually tuned in. But I would miss parts of the instructions, or I’d start the work and then somehow not finish it unless the teacher came by and kind of redirected me or stayed close enough to keep me on track.

And I remember feeling confused sometimes because everyone else seemed to know exactly what we were supposed to be doing, and I’d be like, “Wait, when did she say that?” even though I had been sitting right there. It wasn’t like I was trying to be difficult. I just wouldn’t catch the whole thing unless someone repeated it or checked in with me.
Did you have a lot of excess energy or fidgetiness when you were a child?

I’m honestly not sure. I don’t remember being the kind of kid who was, like, bouncing off the walls or constantly running around in a way adults complained about. At least, I don’t have a strong memory of that, and I don’t think that was the main thing people noticed about me.

I may have fidgeted some, like normal kid stuff — shifting around, messing with things, doodling, that kind of thing — but I don’t know if it was “a lot” or more than other kids. Nobody in my family has really described me that way, like “you were so hyper” or “you could never sit still.” If anything, when I think back, the stuff that stands out more is just… not fully being locked in, rather than having tons of energy.

So I guess my answer is no, not that I can clearly remember. Or at least, if it was there, it wasn’t obvious enough that I was aware of it or that people talked about it much.

target_item.manifestation: My mom still has elementary school report cards from around fourth grade saying I was bright but needed constant reminders to finish classwork and turn in homework. I remember understanding the lessons but missing chunks of instructions unless the teacher stayed close to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether these attention and assignment-completion problems were present during school years, which directly relates to childhood onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I did. I mean, looking back, it was there pretty early, not just something that started as an adult.

My mom actually still has some of my old elementary school report cards, and I remember seeing one from around fourth grade where the teacher basically said I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork and turn in homework. That’s kind of the exact pattern I remember, too. I wasn’t usually confused by the lesson itself. Like, if the teacher explained something and I was actually tuned in, I could understand it. But then when it came time to follow all the directions, or finish the worksheet, or remember to put the homework in the right place and actually hand it in, that’s where things would fall apart.

I remember missing parts of instructions a lot unless the teacher was nearby or kind of checking on me. If she was close to me, I could stay on track better, but if she gave the whole class directions and then moved on, I’d realize halfway through that I had missed a chunk of what we were supposed to do. It was embarrassing, because I didn’t feel like I didn’t know the material. It was more like I lost pieces of the process somewhere between hearing it and actually completing it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like your difficulties with finishing tasks and following through on instructions are causing significant problems in your life outside of work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work this has led to formal retraining meetings, coworkers covering parts of my duties, and real fear that I’ll be moved off the line or fired. I feel like I’m becoming a safety concern instead of the reliable worker I want to be.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the attention-related difficulty with finishing tasks and following through causes significant life problems, which is directly about functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I mean… yes, definitely. The biggest place I notice it is work, honestly, and it’s gotten to the point where it feels serious, not just annoying or like “oh, I’m forgetful.”

I work in a setting where there are steps and instructions that actually matter, and when I don’t finish something all the way or I miss part of what I was told, it doesn’t just affect me. Other people end up having to step in and cover pieces of my duties, or double-check things I should have already done. And that’s embarrassing, because I’m not trying to be careless. I really want to be reliable.

There have been formal retraining meetings because of it, where they go back over procedures with me, and I’ll understand it in the meeting, but then in the actual flow of work I’ll lose track of some part of it or not follow through the way I’m supposed to. It makes me feel like people are watching me like I’m a problem.

And I’m honestly scared I could be moved off the line or even fired if it keeps happening. That’s probably the part that weighs on me the most. I don’t want to be seen as a safety concern, but that’s kind of how it feels sometimes, like instead of being the dependable worker I’m trying to be, I’m becoming someone everyone has to work around.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social relationships due to their symptoms
doctor.question: Have you noticed any problems in your relationships with friends or family that you think might be related to your difficulties with finishing tasks or following instructions?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about relationship problems with friends or family related to symptoms, but the provided profile only describes workplace impairment and does not include social or family relationship impairment.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure, honestly. I haven’t really connected it as clearly with friends or family the way I have with work.

Like, with family, I’m sure there are times where I forget something someone asked me to do, or I don’t follow through right away, but I don’t know if I’d say it’s caused major relationship problems. I guess my family might get annoyed with me sometimes, but I haven’t really thought of it as this big pattern in the same way.

With friends, I don’t know… I don’t think anyone has directly said, like, “you’re a bad friend because you don’t finish things” or anything like that. Maybe there are little things, like if I say I’ll look something up or handle a plan and then I forget, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean. It’s harder for me to separate normal forgetfulness from something that’s actually affecting the relationship.

So I guess my answer is I haven’t noticed it in a major way, or at least no one has really pointed it out to me like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has symptoms of inattention that are persistent across different settings
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or activities when you're not at work?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: Even when I start a shift trying really hard to stay locked in, after a while the cutting, weighing, and checking labels all blur together and I realize I’ve been staring at the same tray or log sheet without taking in what I’m supposed to do next.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty focusing on tasks or activities outside of work, which directly matches sustained attention difficulty.

patient.answer:
Yes… I do. I mean, I notice it most at work because that’s where the consequences are more obvious, but it’s not like my focus problems only switch on when I clock in.

Even when I start a shift telling myself, like, “Okay, today I’m going to stay really locked in, I’m going to pay attention to every step,” after a while everything starts to kind of blend together. The cutting, weighing, checking labels, looking at the tray, looking at the log sheet… it all starts to blur, and then I’ll suddenly realize I’ve just been staring at the same tray or the same paperwork without actually taking in what I’m supposed to do next.

It’s not that I’m choosing not to focus. I’ll be looking right at the thing, but my brain isn’t fully grabbing onto it. Then I have to almost restart in my head and figure out, “Wait, what step was I on? Did I already check that? What was I supposed to do after this?” It’s really frustrating because I can start out trying so hard, and then I still drift off mentally.

doctor.intent: Determine presence of avoidance behavior
doctor.question: Do you often avoid tasks or activities because you feel overwhelmed by them?

target_item.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I put off the certification modules and any long procedure reading until the last possible minute because sitting there trying to absorb all those rules feels almost physically exhausting.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about avoiding tasks or activities because they feel overwhelming, which directly matches reluctance or avoidance of tasks requiring sustained mental effort.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. I think “overwhelmed” is actually a pretty accurate word for it, because it’s not always that the task is technically impossible or even that long, but the amount of mental effort it feels like it’s going to take makes me avoid it.

The biggest example is the certification modules and long procedure readings I’m supposed to do. I put those off until the absolute last possible minute. I’ll know I need to do them, and I’ll even have time, but just the idea of sitting there and trying to absorb all those rules and steps and wording feels almost physically exhausting. Like I’m tired before I even start. I’ll open it and see pages of procedures or training information, and my brain kind of goes, “Nope, not right now,” even if I know avoiding it is going to make things worse later.

And then I end up doing this whole thing where I tell myself I’ll do it after I eat, or after I shower, or when I’m more awake, or on my next day off, and then suddenly it’s right before it’s due and I’m trying to cram through it. It’s frustrating because I’m not avoiding it because I don’t care. I do care. It just feels so heavy to start, especially when I know I have to sit still and actually take in detailed information.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulties are primarily related to attention or if there are other underlying issues such as obsessive-compulsive traits
doctor.question: Do you find yourself spending a lot of time on details, to the point where it slows down your completion of tasks?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about getting overly caught up in details or perfectionism that slows task completion, which is not covered by the listed ADHD inattentive symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure. I don’t think that’s the main thing that slows me down, if that makes sense.

Like, I can get stuck on a detail sometimes if I’m worried I missed something, but I wouldn’t say I’m usually being perfectionistic or spending forever making something exactly right. It’s more that I lose track of where I am, or I have to reread or recheck because I’m not confident I actually took it in the first time.

So… if you mean, do I get so focused on tiny details that I can’t finish because I’m over-polishing everything, I don’t really think so. But if you mean I end up taking longer because I have to keep going back over things or checking what I already did, then maybe sometimes. I just don’t know if that counts as “spending a lot of time on details,” exactly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a history of symptoms consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) that could explain their difficulties with task completion and organization
doctor.question: Did you ever receive a diagnosis of ADHD or have symptoms of ADHD as a child, such as difficulty paying attention or hyperactivity?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: My mom still has elementary school report cards from around fourth grade saying I was bright but needed constant reminders to finish classwork and turn in homework. I remember understanding the lessons but missing chunks of instructions unless the teacher stayed close to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether ADHD symptoms were present in childhood, which directly maps to onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
I was never officially diagnosed as a kid, no. At least not that I know of. But looking back, there were definitely signs, especially with paying attention.

My mom actually still has some of my old elementary school report cards, and I remember one from around fourth grade saying something like I was bright, but I needed constant reminders to finish my classwork and turn in homework. That kind of sums up a lot of it, honestly. I wasn’t a kid who didn’t understand what was being taught. I usually did understand the lesson once I was actually tuned in. But I would miss parts of the instructions, or I’d start the work and then somehow not finish it unless the teacher came by and kind of redirected me or stayed close enough to keep me on track.

And I remember feeling confused sometimes because everyone else seemed to know exactly what we were supposed to be doing, and I’d be like, “Wait, when did she say that?” even though I had been sitting right there. It wasn’t like I was trying to be difficult. I just wouldn’t catch the whole thing unless someone repeated it or checked in with me.

doctor.question: Did you have a lot of excess energy or fidgetiness when you were a child?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about childhood hyperactivity or fidgetiness, but the symptom profile only covers inattentive symptoms and childhood onset of attention-related difficulties, not excess energy or fidgetiness.

patient.answer:
I’m honestly not sure. I don’t remember being the kind of kid who was, like, bouncing off the walls or constantly running around in a way adults complained about. At least, I don’t have a strong memory of that, and I don’t think that was the main thing people noticed about me.

I may have fidgeted some, like normal kid stuff — shifting around, messing with things, doodling, that kind of thing — but I don’t know if it was “a lot” or more than other kids. Nobody in my family has really described me that way, like “you were so hyper” or “you could never sit still.” If anything, when I think back, the stuff that stands out more is just… not fully being locked in, rather than having tons of energy.

So I guess my answer is no, not that I can clearly remember. Or at least, if it was there, it wasn’t obvious enough that I was aware of it or that people talked about it much.
